candidate.answerReason: Extending the perpendicular at A to line BC creates a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 6. The resulting larger right triangle has long leg 10 and short leg CD, so CD=10/√3.

methods.label: Create two special right triangles
methods.explanation:
Extend the perpendicular at \(A\) until it meets line \(BC\) at \(T\). These lines meet because a line perpendicular to \(AB\) cannot be parallel to \(BC\) when \(\angle ABC=120^\circ\).

The point \(T\) must lie beyond \(B\), on the side opposite \(C\). Otherwise triangle \(ABT\) would have both a \(120^\circ\) angle at \(B\) and a right angle at \(A\), which is impossible. Hence
\[
\angle ABT=60^\circ,\qquad \angle ATB=30^\circ.
\]
In a right triangle, the side opposite \(30^\circ\) is half the hypotenuse. Thus
\[
TB=2AB=6.
\]
Since \(T,B,C\) occur in that order, \(TC=6+4=10\).

The line \(TD\) is the same line as \(TA\), so right triangle \(TCD\) also has a \(30^\circ\) angle at \(T\). Therefore \(TD=2CD\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to this larger triangle gives
\[
TC^2=TD^2-CD^2
=(2CD)^2-CD^2=3CD^2.
\]
Because \(CD>0\),
\[
CD=\frac{10}{\sqrt3},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
methods.levelReason: The construction reduces the problem to the half-hypotenuse property for a 30° angle and the Pythagorean theorem.
